title: Causal Estimation of Share-Induced Engagement with Flywheel Effects

problem.claim: Online platforms need to measure engagement generated by sharing features that can reactivate users and propagate engagement through social networks.

gap.claim: Classical A/B-testing estimators are inadequate when sharing effects spread through network interference and temporal cascades.

contributions.claim: A framework is developed for experiments on sharing features that targets a global treatment effect while accounting for flywheel-induced interference.
The proposed estimator uses a flow-balance identity and closed-form propagation adjustment to model multi-round share-induced engagement from attribution logs.

The work establishes estimator consistency under mild conditions, provides an A/A validation procedure, extends the approach to user-level reactivation, and demonstrates it on a large-scale online platform.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Simulations reportedly show lower bias than difference-in-means and first-order adjustment estimators.
The proposed A/A test reportedly maintains nominal Type I error in simulations.
A real-world large-scale online-platform application is reported, with empirical implications for sharing-feature evaluation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Platform growth depends on both acquiring users and re-engaging existing users through sharing.
Sharing can create multi-round network amplification as reactivated users become additional sharers.
Network interference and temporal cascades make causal measurement difficult for conventional experiments.
The paper introduces an interference-aware framework and propagation-adjusted estimator for global share-induced engagement.
The abstract reports theoretical guarantees, simulation results, a reactivation extension, and a real-world demonstration.

source_observation.claim: Spillover effects can accumulate across multiple rounds and invalidate no-interference assumptions.

interpretation.claim: Experiments for networked product features may need estimands and adjustments that represent propagation rather than isolated individual treatment effects.

application.claim: Use propagation-aware causal measurement when evaluating sharing or referral mechanisms with cascading downstream engagement.

exception.claim: The approach may depend on attribution logs and the stated mild conditions, whose precise requirements are not specified in the abstract.

unknowns: Precise estimand definition and mathematical form of the estimator
Exact assumptions constituting the stated mild conditions
Simulation design, datasets, sample sizes, and quantitative effect sizes
Details of the real-world platform, deployment, and evaluation protocol
